label: AQ 0012
title: The comment that gave the orders

questions.q: Couldn't a second model screen every comment first?
questions.a: As one layer, yes. As the wall, no. Willison is wary of guardrail products that claim to stop 95% of attacks, because “in web application security 95% is very much a failing grade.” The 12 defences in the Nasr et al. study included detectors of this kind.

teach.title: How it works: moving the control out of the prompt

questions.q: What if the owner really wants to change the agent's goal?
questions.a: Through a channel only the owner controls: editing the file, or approving a change the agent proposes. A comment can at most become a suggestion awaiting review.
A close cousin. The trifecta is about leaking data; here the danger is a shell command. Same fix: never let untrusted text sit next to a powerful tool with nothing in between.

questions.q: Why can't the model enforce “only obey the owner” by itself?
questions.a: The rule and the comment reach it the same way, as text in one context. It can't reliably tell who wrote which, and a look-alike name is just more text.

questions.q: Name three controls that live outside the model.
questions.a: The comment-reading step has no shell tool; the instruction files are read-only to the agent; risky commands need a person's approval.

teach.title: How it works: moving the control out of the prompt

questions.q: Prompt defences held fixed attacks to about 1% success. Why isn't that reassuring?
questions.a: Real attackers adapt. When the attack was tuned against each defence, success rose above 95%. The attacker moves second.
